walkthroughs.body_html:
Paper 1: Poetry and Prose — a core area of GCSE English Literature.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Paper 1: Poetry and Prose brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Paper 1: Poetry and Prose.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Why distinguish the speaker of a poem from the poet?
options: The speaker is the voice constructed in the poem; the poet is the writer. Treating them as identical can mislead, especially with dramatic monologues or personae.
The speaker is whoever reads the poem out loud.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
The speaker of a poem is always the poet themselves.
Enjambment is when a poem has very long lines.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
Enjambment is when a poem uses no punctuation at all.
When a sentence or phrase runs over from one line of poetry to the next without a punctuated pause, creating flow or surprise across the line break.

mcqs.q: Why must students distinguish the narrator from the author?
options: The narrator's views are always the author's views.
The narrator is a constructed voice within the text; the author is the real person who created it. Conflating them misreads irony, unreliable narration and persona.
The speaker is whoever reads the poem out loud.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
